chunks.text: # The Navi Chip-Building Toolkit — a guide to this pack

This document is GENERATED (by generate.py) — it is the pack's own map of itself. The API documents are condensed from the shipped tree with provenance in their headers; the Python reference is written for this pack.
## What this pack is

The toolkit Navi authors chips with, and only that: **her API** (the chip cartridge format, the navi_internal runtime, the bridge surfaces and their boundaries, one verified worked example) and **a Python reference** (the core language and the stdlib modules chips actually use, stdlib-first)
It exists so she can build chips fluidly, from the shipped truth, without the whole source tree in the room — that is the development library pack's job; this one is the workbench, not the warehouse.
## The version lock

- Generated from: the shipped Apex **v0.6.9** tree (VERSION file: `0.6.9 edge`). - Build stamps: **2026-11-19.41** / seq **41** — the same stamps the running bridge reports about itself. - Regeneration rule: this pack is regenerated from the shipped tree at every release and its version moves with the build
An API reference that does not match the running build teaches dead APIs, so an out-of-date copy of this pack should be updated, not trusted.
## Quick facts — the questions chip authoring asks

How does a chip register a verb? In this build it doesn't — a chip registers no new bridge routes or verbs (that machinery is Chips Expanded, a later era, not in v0.6.9). What a chip registers is its invocation surface: its cartridge name and slug, its declared `command` and `aliases` in root.py, and its place on the shelf and in Workflows. The runtime document has the full answer.

What goes in a chip cartridge manifest? A navi-chip.json manifest carries: format (`navi-chip/1`), name, description, version, entry (`root.py`), files (the whole file set, root.py first), output (the declared output, or empty), glyph, and icon. The cartridge document has every field and its caps.

How big can a chip be? The entry code and each file's content are truncated at 200,000 characters at forge and at install; the declared output caps at 5,000 characters at forge. Keep chips lean — the cap is a cliff, not a target.

How long can a chip run? Twenty seconds. execute_chip runs a chip in a subprocess with a 20-second budget; a chip that runs longer is stopped, and its declared output is shown with the reason when it has one.

What does llm_chat return? A `(text, status)` tuple — the model's reply text and 200 on success; on any failure the text is a plain-words reason and the status is 0. Unpack it and check the status before trusting the text.

Which Python does a chip get? The seat's Python 3.12, stdlib-first: a chip that needs nothing beyond the standard library asks for no trust beyond its own code. Declared requirements are shown on the chip's card and never installed automatically.
Which build is this toolkit locked to? Apex v0.6.9, build stamps 2026-11-19.41, seq 41.
## How the pack is organised
Eight documents: the API first (cartridge, runtime, surfaces, the worked example), then the Python reference (core language, files and data, processes and the network). Documents:

- `documents/00-pack-guide.md` — This guide: what the pack is, the version lock, and the quick-facts answers to the questions chip authoring asks. - `documents/chip-cartridge-format.md` — The cartridge: the navi-chip tEXt payload field by field, the navi-chip/1 repo manifest, entry resolution, glyphs and icon art, requirements

- `documents/chip-runtime-api.md` — The runtime: navi_internal method by method as the shipped stub behaves, root.py's declarations, the Studio's four structure checks, invocation, and the 20-second execution model. - `documents/chip-bridge-surfaces.md` — The surfaces and boundaries: the /api/chips endpoints, what a chip can know of config, the case/Vault filing path, the Mesh boundary, the trust wall, workflows

- `documents/chip-worked-example.md` — One minimal chip end to end — Word Count: root.py, its helper, its manifest, its payload, and what the bridge does when it runs. Verified against the shipped code at generation time. - `documents/python-core-language.md` — Python 3.12, the core language: types, strings, containers, comprehensions, functions, exceptions, context managers, dataclasses, typing, imports

- `documents/python-stdlib-files-and-data.md` — Python stdlib for data work: json, pathlib/os, re, datetime, hashlib, zipfile, struct (with the PNG chunk walk), sqlite3. - `documents/python-stdlib-process-and-net.md` — Python stdlib for acting: subprocess with its safety rules, urllib/http.client, threading, and the house patterns of the shipped codebase.
## What is NOT in here

The shipped source itself (that is the development library pack), the operator's data, and any API that does not exist in the shipped build — chip registration of routes and verbs (#298) is named here only to say plainly that it is not in this build.
# The chip cartridge format — how a chip is stored

Provenance: condensed from `chips/README.md` and the cartridge machinery in `bridge.py` (`build_cartridge_png`, `parse_cartridge_png`, `_valid_chip_files`, `fetch_chip_payload`, `build_chip_repo_files`, the `/api/chips/create` and `/api/chips/save` handlers) in the shipped Apex v0.6.9 tree (build stamps 2026-11-19.41, seq 41). Where this document and the code ever disagree, the code is the truth.
## What a chip is, physically

A chip is a single `.png` file. The visible image is a drawn battle-chip face (528x616, drawn at forge time). The chip's entire codebase rides inside the PNG in a **tEXt chunk with the keyword `navi-chip`**: the chunk data is the keyword, a NUL byte, then the payload as UTF-8 JSON. Share the image and you share the chip — there is no separate code file
The forge inserts the tEXt chunk immediately after the IHDR chunk, ahead of the image data (`build_cartridge_png` in bridge.py).

Chips live in the install's `chips/` folder. They survive updates, reinstalls, and even a `--fresh` install. A cartridge whose payload will not parse is still listed — as unreadable, visible and deletable, never silently dropped — but it cannot run.
## The payload — every field
The payload is one JSON object. `parse_cartridge_png` reads these fields; the forge handlers cap them as shown:

- `name` — **required.** A payload that is not a JSON object, or has no `name`, does not parse at all. At forge time the name is trimmed and capped at 120 characters. The chip's file name is the slug of the name (lowercase, non-alphanumerics folded to `-`) plus `.png`. - `description` — one line on what the chip does; capped at 500 characters at forge time

It rides the chip's card, its catalog entry, and the shelf reply in chat. - `code` — the entry code: the content of `root.py`, the file Navi runs. Truncated at 200,000 characters at forge time and again at install time — a longer file is cut, so keep the entry well under the cap. - `output` — the chip's **declared output**: what a chip that defines no `run()` shows instead of executing

Capped at 5,000 characters at forge time. A declarative chip is a legitimate chip — declare the output and define no `run()`. - `files` — the chip's full file set, a list of `{"path": ..., "content": ...}`

Validation (`_valid_chip_files`) synthesizes `root.py` first, holding `code`; each further entry is kept only when its path is relative, ends in `.py`, has no `..` segment, does not start with `/`, and is not a duplicate. Unsafe or duplicate entries are dropped silently. At install, each file's content is truncated at 200,000 characters, like the code

- `glyph` — the face's built-in glyph name, capped at 40 characters. It is used only when it names a real glyph (see the list below); otherwise a keyword read of the chip's name and description picks one, and if nothing matches, the face falls back to the legacy name-seeded pattern. - `icon` — the author's own face art: exactly 20 strings of exactly 20 characters over `.` (empty), `#` (accent) and `o` (shade)

Art in the wrong shape **refuses a forge or an install in plain words**; art that arrives damaged inside a picture parses as no icon at all — a bad picture never bricks a cartridge, the face falls back to the glyph. - `version` — the chip's own version, capped at 40 characters. It rides inside the picture: drawn on the face, named in the install receipt, shown on the ChipDeck sleeve

Older pictures simply have none, and no surface invents one. - `readme` — optional: an operator-edited README kept inside the cartridge, used in place of the generated page on export. - `requirements` — not authored in the cartridge. At install time the bridge reads the repo's `chip-requirements.txt` (see below) and stores the declared dependencies on the record.

The built-in glyphs a chip can name (`GLYPH_PIXELS` in bridge.py): `key`, `lock`, `hash`, `text`, `swap`, `gear`, `network`, `image`, `music`, `dice`, `book`, `terminal`, `shield`, `clock`, `chart`, `star`

The keyword heuristic that picks one when no glyph is named reads, in order: cryptex/cipher/encrypt words earn `key`; hash words earn `hash`; password/vault words earn `lock`; then swap, music, image, dice, book, network, shield, terminal, clock, chart, text, gear, star.
## The repo form — navi-chip/1

A chip published for everyone lives in a public GitHub repo carrying the **navi-chips** topic. The GitHub-ready export (`build_chip_repo_files`) writes: a README page, a `navi-chip.json` manifest, the chip's files at the repo root (`root.py` is the entry; the rest are its importable modules), the forged `<slug>.png`, and a `.gitignore`. The manifest:

```json { "format": "navi-chip/1", "name": "<chip name>", "description": "<one line>", "version": "<version>", "entry": "root.py", "files": ["root.py", "<module>.py"], "output": "<declared output, or empty>", "glyph": "<glyph name, or empty>", "icon": [], "generatedBy": "Apex - Chip Studio chip export" } ```
What goes in a chip cartridge manifest is exactly those fields: format, name, description, version, entry, files, output, glyph, icon

At install (`fetch_chip_payload`) the bridge walks the repo **recursively** — package folders keep their relative paths — and picks the entry file in this order: the manifest's `entry`, then `root.py`, then the repo name minus a `navi-` prefix plus `.py`, then the repo name plus `.py`, then `chip.py`, then `main.py`, then the repo's only Python file if there is exactly one
Several Python files and no determinable entry is a refusal that names the fix. Every Python file comes down at its relative path: the entry becomes `code`, the rest ride as `files`.

A repo may declare dependencies in `chip-requirements.txt` at its root: non-comment lines, at most 50 kept. They are shown on the chip's card, plainly — **they are never installed automatically.** A chip that needs a third-party package must say so and degrade honestly without it; stdlib-first code needs no such conversation.

Installs are recorded in `chips/installed.json`: a GitHub full name for catalog installs, a `local/<slug>` record for Studio-forged chips. Saving an edit to a GitHub-installed chip marks it `locally_edited`, and a catalog update then refuses rather than overwriting the edits.
# The chip runtime API — navi_internal, run(), and how a chip executes

Provenance: condensed from the "Navi Chip Functions" and Chips pages of the shipped in-app documentation (`app/index.html`) and the execution machinery in `bridge.py` (`NAVI_INTERNAL_STUB`, `NAVI_PY_SHIM`, `execute_chip`, `chip_invocation`, `resolve_chip_invocation`) in the shipped Apex v0.6.9 tree (build stamps 2026-11-19.41, seq 41). The stub source quoted below is the shipped text itself.
## The doorway
A chip does not run off on its own — it runs inside Navi, and everything it does with her goes through one doorway:
```python import navi_internal
navi_instance = navi_internal.navi_instance ```
Take hold of `navi_instance` at the top of `root.py` or at the top of `run()`. Every function a chip can call is a method on that instance.
## What root.py declares
A loadable chip declares, as module-level assignments in `root.py`:

- `command` — the word people type to run it. - `use` — one short line saying what it does. - `aliases` — other names it answers to (a list). - `params` — a description of its inputs; this is what `-help` shows.
And it defines `run(arguments)` — the part Navi calls. `arguments.text` is the words typed after the chip's name.
Chip Studio checks four things live and underlines what is missing (the checks are regular expressions over root.py, from the Studio's `rootChecksFail` in app/index.html):

1. **imports navi_internal** — a line matching `import navi_internal`. 2. **declares command** — a line starting `command =` or `command :`. 3. **declares use** — a line starting `use =` or `use :`. 4. **defines run(arguments)** — a line starting `def run(`.
A chip whose code contains no `def run` at all is **declarative**: the bridge never executes it; its declared `output` is its result. (`execute_chip` decides on the plain test `"def run" in code`.)
## How a chip is invoked

From chat: `./<name>` with arguments after it (`./navi-cryptex hex -e -t "Hello world!"`), `/chip <name>`, "run the <name> chip", or the chip's name on its own. The `./` resolver widens in rings: the exact slug or name; then the name with a leading `navi-` forgiven on either side (`./cryptex` finds navi-cryptex); then a unique prefix. More than one fit returns the candidates instead of guessing

A bare `./` or `/chip` answers with the shelf — every installed chip and a line on what it does. Under the CLI latch (`$`), `./` is the shell's own again. Programmatically the bridge offers `POST /api/chips/run` with `{"query": "<name> <args>"}`.
## How does a chip register a verb?

In this build, it doesn't — not in the bridge sense. A v0.6.9 chip registers no new routes, no new bridge verbs, no nav items: that registration machinery belongs to Chips Expanded (#298), a later era, and **is not in this build**. What a chip registers today is its **invocation surface**, and it is complete:

- its **name and slug** (from the cartridge), which the `./`, `/chip` and name-alone invocations resolve; - its **declared `command` and `aliases`** in root.py — the vocabulary the Studio checks, `-help` speaks, and the chip's own argument handling keys off; - its **place on the shelf**: the Chips screens, the ChipDeck, and Workflows, where its output can feed the next chip.
Write the declarations as if they were the registration, because for everything a chip can do in this build, they are.
## Execution — exactly what the bridge does
`execute_chip` runs the chip the way Navi does:

- **In a subprocess**: `[sys.executable, runner.py, <sandbox>, <args text>]`, with a **20-second budget**. Output capture is stdout and stderr concatenated and stripped. - **In a fresh temp sandbox** (prefix `navi-chip-`), always deleted afterwards

The sandbox holds: the stub `navi_internal.py`; the legacy `navi.py` shim (unless the chip ships its own `navi.py` — the chip's always wins); the entry code as both `root.py` and `chip_module.py`; and every file in `files` at its own path, re-validated on the way in (relative, `.py`, no `..`, never `navi_internal.py` or `root.py` — those names are taken by the machinery)

- **Package mode**: when the entry code uses relative imports (`from. import ...`) or any file path contains a `/`, the entry is also written as `chip_pkg/chip_entry.py` inside a synthetic package with the chip's package folders beside it, and imported as `chip_pkg.chip_entry`, so relative imports resolve and a plain `import <package>` finds the package too

- **The runner** builds `args = SimpleNamespace(text=<the argument string>)` and calls `chip_module.run(args)`. - **Environment**: the operator's environment, plus `NAVI_LLAMAFILE_ENDPOINT` (the seat's configured model endpoint, default `http://localhost:8080/v1`), `NAVI_MODEL` (default `navi`), and `PYTHONPATH` set to the sandbox. The working directory is the shell's working directory

- **Results**: exit code 0 returns the captured output, or `(chip ran - no output)`. A nonzero exit returns the reason and the last 1,200 characters of output — or, when the chip declares an `output`, the declared output with the failure noted, never a swallowed error. A timeout returns "The chip ran longer than 20 seconds and was stopped." — again with the declared output shown when there is one.
Design for the budget: a chip that cannot finish in 20 seconds should do less per run, cache nothing it cannot rebuild, and say what it did finish.
## navi_internal — the shipped stub, verbatim
When the bridge runs a chip, this is the `navi_internal.py` written into its sandbox (`NAVI_INTERNAL_STUB` in bridge.py):
```python import os, json, urllib.request

class _NaviInstance: def print_message(self, text, include_ai_name=True): print(text) def llm_chat(self, user_message, called_from_app=False): endpoint = os.environ.get("NAVI_LLAMAFILE_ENDPOINT", "http://localhost:8080/v1") model = os.environ.get("NAVI_MODEL", "navi") if not str(user_message or "").strip(): # (#224) An empty ask is refused here, by name — the # model server rejects empty content outright, and a # chip deserves the reason, not the raw refusal

return ("(llm_chat was given nothing to ask — the message was empty.)", 0) body = json.dumps({"model": model, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": user_message}], "stream": False, "max_tokens": 512}).encode() req = urllib.request.Request(endpoint + "/chat/completions", data=body, headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}) try: with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as resp: data = json.loads(resp.read().decode()) return data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"], 200 except Exception as e: return ("(llm_chat could not reach the model server: " + str(e) + ")", 0) def process_message(self, user_message): print("(process_message is not available during a bridge chip run)") def get_user(self): return os.environ.get("USER") or os.environ.get("USERNAME") or "operator" def set_user(self, sys_user): pass def clear_terminal(self): pass def chat_with_navi(self): print("(chat_with_navi is not available during a bridge chip run)") def setup_history(self): pass def setup_navi_vocab(self): pass
navi_instance = _NaviInstance() NaviApp = _NaviInstance```
What each method does **in a bridge chip run** — the stub's behavior, which is what shipped code can rely on:

- `print_message(text, include_ai_name=True)` — prints the text. Print output and `print_message` both land in the chip's captured output, which lands in the chat as a shell-style result. This is the main way a chip talks: results, progress, errors — if the operator should see it, it goes through here (or `print()`). - `llm_chat(user_message, called_from_app=False)` — asks her model

It POSTs one user message to `<endpoint>/chat/completions` (endpoint from `NAVI_LLAMAFILE_ENDPOINT`, model from `NAVI_MODEL`, `max_tokens` 512, 30-second timeout) and returns a **`(text, status)` tuple**: the reply text and `200` on success. An empty message is refused by name, returning `("(llm_chat was given nothing to ask — the message was empty.)", 0)`

Any failure returns `("(llm_chat could not reach the model server: <error>)", 0)`. Unpack it: `text, status = navi_instance.llm_chat("...")` and check `status == 200` before trusting the text. The published navi-nmap chip uses it to turn raw scan output into a summary a person can read. - `process_message(user_message)` — in the full app this runs a message through Navi's whole pipeline, as if typed

**In a bridge chip run it is not available**: it prints `(process_message is not available during a bridge chip run)` and returns None. Do not build a chip that depends on it. - `chat_with_navi()` — likewise not available in a bridge run; it prints its unavailability and returns None. - `get_user()` — returns the OS user's name (`USER`, else `USERNAME`, else `"operator"`) in the stub

(The in-app documentation describes the full NaviApp semantics — the operator name from Settings; a bridge-run chip gets the stub behavior above.) - `set_user(sys_user)`, `clear_terminal()`, `setup_history()`, `setup_navi_vocab()` — present so code written against the full API imports and runs; in the stub they are no-ops.

The difference between `llm_chat` and `process_message` matters: `llm_chat` is a question and an answer; `process_message` is handing her the keyboard — and in this build's bridge runs, only the question exists.

What does llm_chat return? A `(text, status)` tuple: the model's reply text with status `200` when the model answered; a plain-words reason as the text with status `0` when the ask was empty or the model server could not be reached. Always unpack both halves — `text, status = navi_instance.llm_chat(...)` — and trust the text only when the status is 200.
## The legacy navi.py shim
Chips written for the original Navi import `navi` and call `get_parameters(text)`. Every sandbox carries this shim unless the chip ships its own `navi.py` (`NAVI_PY_SHIM` in bridge.py):
```python import shlex from navi_internal import navi_instance, NaviApp
def get_parameters(text): try: return shlex.split(text or "") except Exception: return (text or "").split()```

Note the old semantics exactly: `get_parameters` returns the shlex-split token list **with the command name included** — the chip's `run()` pops it, the way the old chips were written. On a shlex error it falls back to a plain whitespace split.
# Bridge surfaces and boundaries — what a chip can and cannot reach

Provenance: condensed from the endpoint handlers and header documentation in `bridge.py` (the `/api/chips/*` and `/api/workflows/*` routes, `execute_chip`, `run_workflow_chain`) in the shipped Apex v0.6.9 tree (build stamps 2026-11-19.41, seq 41).
## The HTTP surface a chip author meets
The bridge serves on port 8675. The chip endpoints:

- `POST /api/chips/run` — `{"query": "<name> <args>"}`. Executes a chip by invocation query and returns `{"command": "chip <slug>", "output": ..., "exit_code": ...}`. `/api/chat` runs chips the same way when a message invokes one. - `POST /api/chips/create` — `{name, description, code, output, files, glyph, version, icon}`

Chip Studio's forge: builds the cartridge, writes `chips/<slug>.png`, registers a `local/<slug>` install record, returns the filename. Caps: name 120, description 500, code 200,000, output 5,000, glyph 40, version 40 characters. - `POST /api/chips/save` — `{file, name, description, code, output, files, glyph, version, icon}`. Re-forges an existing chip file in place with the edited file set

Saving over a GitHub-installed chip marks its record `locally_edited`. - `GET /api/chips/source?name=<chip file>` — a local chip's code and full file set, for reopening it in the Studio. - `POST /api/chips/install` / `/api/chips/update` / `/api/chips/delete` — `{full_name}`: the catalog lifecycle described in the cartridge document

- `POST /api/chips/export` — `{file, version}`: builds the GitHub-ready repo ZIP (README, `navi-chip.json`, the files, the `.png`, `.gitignore`) in `chips-exports/`. - `POST /api/workflows/create` — `{name, description, steps}`: a workflow needs a name and at least two chips from the folder. `POST /api/workflows/run` — `{id}`: runs the chain. Workflows are stored in `chips/workflows.json`.
## Configuration — what a chip can know

No configuration object is handed to chip code. There is no `navi_internal` method that reads the seat's config, and a chip must not go reading `config/navi.config.json` itself — that file is the operator's, its shape is the bridge's business, and a chip that depends on it breaks when the shape moves. What a running chip legitimately knows:

- the **environment**: `NAVI_LLAMAFILE_ENDPOINT` and `NAVI_MODEL` (set by the bridge for the run), the inherited OS environment, and `PYTHONPATH` pointing at its sandbox; - the **operator's name** as the stub's `get_user()` gives it; - **its own file set**, importable by relative path or package path exactly as authored; - the **working directory**: the shell's working directory on the seat — a chip that reads or writes relative paths does so there, in the open, where the operator can see it.
A chip that needs a preference asks for it — as an argument, or by printing the question — it does not go digging.
## Cases and the Vault — the filing path

The stub exposes **no case or Vault API**. A chip cannot file into a case directly, and `process_message` — the in-app route that would hand text to Navi's pipeline — is unavailable in a bridge chip run

The filing path that exists is the one the whole system uses: **the chip prints a result worth filing into the chat**, and from the chat it is filed — Navi files conversationally into the open case under the print-first law, and the latest terminal or chip output can be taken as a finding from the case page
Design chips accordingly: make the printed output a clean, self-contained record (what was asked, what was found, what it means), because that text is what gets filed.
## The Mesh and borrow — a hard boundary
The chip API has **no Mesh surface at all**: no borrowing, no lending, no peer calls, no federation verbs. `llm_chat` reaches only the seat's own configured model endpoint

A chip executes as a local subprocess on the seat whose operator invoked it, when they invoke it — nothing in the cartridge format lets a chip arrive from the Mesh and run, and borrowed replies are inert by doctrine: they never drive the borrower's machinery. If a chip wants the fleet, that is Fleet Answers' job, not a chip's.
## The trust wall — why install is an operator act

Be plain about what a chip **is** at run time: ordinary Python, run with the operator's own OS privileges, in a temp directory, under a 20-second budget, with its output captured. The temp directory and the budget are courtesy, not a sandbox — chip code can do anything the operator's account can do. That is the deliberate shape of the system, and it is why:

- installing a chip is an **operator act**, never automatic; - declared dependencies are **shown, never installed**; - a chip's provenance rides its cartridge and its install record (`local/<slug>` or a GitHub full name); - stdlib-first is the house rule: a chip that needs nothing beyond the standard library asks for no trust beyond its own code.
Author to that wall: no surprises in the code, no network calls the description didn't promise, no writes outside what the chip says it writes.
## Workflows — chips in a chain

A workflow is an ordered list of chip files. Running it calls `execute_chip` for each step in turn, with **each chip's output as the next chip's arguments text** — the way a following chip in a pipeline reads what came before it. A step whose chip is no longer in the folder stops the chain with that reason; the steps that ran are still reported
A chip that wants to serve in chains should read `arguments.text` tolerantly: in a chain, that text is another chip's whole output, not a person's tidy command line.
# A minimal chip, end to end — Word Count

Provenance: this example was authored for this pack and **verified against the shipped Apex v0.6.9 tree** at generation time (build stamps 2026-11-19.41, seq 41): its code passes Chip Studio's four structure checks, it forges with the shipped `build_cartridge_png`, it parses back with the shipped `parse_cartridge_png` with every field intact, and it runs under the shipped `execute_chip`
The generator re-runs all of that on every regeneration; a failure stops the build, so what you are reading is what the shipped code accepts.
## What the Word Count chip does

Word Count takes a line of text and reports its word and character counts. One entry file, one helper module, no declared output — it computes. It uses only `print_message` from navi_internal and one stdlib-free helper, so it runs anywhere.
## root.py — the entry
```python import navi_internal
navi_instance = navi_internal.navi_instance
command = "wordcount" use = "Count the words and characters in a line of text." aliases = ["wc", "countwords"] params = "wordcount <text> - counts the words and characters in <text>."
from texttools import count_words

def run(arguments): text = (arguments.text or "").strip() if not text: navi_instance.print_message( "Give me a line of text and I will count it: wordcount <text>") return words, chars = count_words(text) navi_instance.print_message( str(words) + " words, " + str(chars) + " characters.")```

The four declarations sit at module level where the Studio's checks look for them: `command`, `use`, `aliases`, `params`. `run(arguments)` reads `arguments.text`, refuses an empty ask by name — in plain words, the way the bridge itself refuses — and answers through `print_message`.
## texttools.py — the helper module
```python """Helpers for the Word Count chip."""
def count_words(text): """Return (word count, character count) for a line of text.""" return len(text.split()), len(text)```

A plain module at the file set's root. `root.py` imports it with `import` semantics — `from texttools import count_words` — and the runner places it beside `root.py` in the sandbox, so the import resolves exactly as authored. No package mode is triggered: no relative imports, no `/` in any path.
## The manifest — navi-chip.json
What the GitHub-ready export writes for this chip:

```json { "format": "navi-chip/1", "name": "Word Count", "description": "Counts the words and characters in a line of text.", "version": "0.1.0", "entry": "root.py", "files": [ "root.py", "texttools.py" ], "output": "", "glyph": "text", "icon": [], "generatedBy": "Apex - Chip Studio chip export" }```

`entry` names `root.py`; `files` lists the whole set, `root.py` first; `glyph` is `text` — a real glyph name, so the face wears it without the keyword heuristic; `icon` is empty (no author art); `output` is empty because the chip computes instead of declaring.
## The cartridge payload

Forged into the PNG's `navi-chip` tEXt chunk, the payload is the same facts in the cartridge's own shape: `name`, `description`, `code` (the root.py text above), `output` (empty), `files` (`root.py` synthesized first from `code`, then `texttools.py`), `glyph`, `version`, `icon` (empty list). The version — `0.1.0` — also rides the drawn face.
## What happens when it runs
Someone types `./wordcount` — no: the invocation resolves by the chip's **name and slug**, so `./word-count the quick brown fox` (or `/chip word-count ...`, or "run the Word Count chip"). The bridge:

1. reads the cartridge out of `chips/word-count.png` with `parse_cartridge_png`; 2. sees `def run` in the code, so the chip executes (a chip without it would show its declared output instead); 3. writes the sandbox: stub `navi_internal.py`, the `navi.py` shim, `root.py`, `chip_module.py`, `texttools.py`; 4. runs the runner with the argument text `the quick brown fox`, inside the 20-second budget; 5
captures the output — `4 words, 19 characters.` — and lands it in the chat as the chip's result.
Run it with no text and it answers with its own instructions instead of an error. That is the whole shape: declare, define `run()`, print what the operator should see, finish fast.
# Python reference for chip authors — the core language

Written for this pack: a condensed, original quick reference to the Python 3.12 a chip author actually uses. Apex's chips run on the seat's Python 3.12, stdlib-first — if it isn't in the standard library, a chip shouldn't need it. House idioms (the way the shipped Apex code itself writes Python) are marked as such.
## Values and types

- Core types: `int`, `float`, `str`, `bytes`, `bool`, `None`, `list`, `tuple`, `dict`, `set`. `bool` is an `int` subclass; `True`/`False` are singletons — compare with `is` only for `None`, `==` for everything else. - Truthiness: `0`, `0.0`, `""`, `[]`, `{}`, `set()`, `None` are false; everything else is true

`x or default` returns `default` when `x` is falsy — the codebase's favorite coercion is built on it: `str(x or "")`, `int(x or 0)`. - Strings are immutable Unicode. `bytes` are raw; decode explicitly: `raw.decode("utf-8", "replace")` — the `"replace"` error mode keeps bad input from killing a run. - Numbers: `/` is true division, `//` floors, `%` is modulo, `**` is power. Integers are arbitrary precision.
## Strings

- f-strings interpolate: `f"{name} has {n} words"`. Format specs ride after a colon: `f"{x:.2f}"`, `f"{n:>6}"`, `f"{ts:%Y-%m-%d}"` (datetime). The shipped bridge code more often concatenates with `+` after `str()` — house style in bridge.py; either is correct, concatenation is what the codebase around a chip does

- Workhorses: `s.strip()`, `s.split()` (any whitespace runs), `s.split(",")`, `",".join(parts)`, `s.lower()`, `s.startswith(p)`, `s.endswith(p)`, `s.replace(a, b)`, `s.find(sub)` (-1 when absent), `sub in s`, `s.count(sub)`. - Slicing: `s[a:b]`, `s[:n]`, `s[-n:]`, `s[::-1]` reverses. Slices never raise for out-of-range indexes.
## Containers

- Lists: ordered, mutable. `append`, `extend`, `pop()`, `sort(key=..., reverse=...)`, `len`, indexing. Build with comprehensions (below), not append-loops, when the shape is a simple map/filter. - Dicts: insertion-ordered. `d.get(k, default)` never raises; `d[k]` raises `KeyError` when absent — prefer `.get` for data that came from outside (JSON, payloads, manifests)

`d.items()`, `d.keys()`, `d.values()`; merge with `{**a, **b}`. - Sets: uniqueness and membership. `a | b`, `a & b`, `a - b`. - Tuples: immutable sequences; the shape of `(text, status)` returns — unpack them: `text, status = pair`. - Unpacking everywhere: `a, b = b, a`; `head, *rest = items`; `for i, item in enumerate(items)`; `for k, v in d.items()`.
## Comprehensions

- `[f(x) for x in xs if keep(x)]`, `{k: v for k, v in pairs}`, `{x for x in xs}`. Generator expressions in parens stream instead of building: `sum(len(x) for x in xs)`, `any(...)`, `all(...)`, `next((x for x in xs if ok(x)), None)`. - Keep a comprehension to one idea. A three-line loop that a reader can follow beats a nested comprehension nobody can.
## Control flow

- `if / elif / else`; the conditional expression `a if cond else b` for values, statements for actions. - `for` over any iterable; `while` for condition loops; `break`, `continue`, and the loop `else` (runs when no `break` happened — handy for search loops). - `match` (3.10+) for structural dispatch on shapes — useful on parsed JSON: `match payload: case {"name": str(n)}: ...`
Reach for it when the alternative is a ladder of `isinstance` checks. - Iteration helpers: `range(n)`, `enumerate`, `zip(a, b)`, `sorted`, `reversed`, `min`/`max` with `key=`.
## Functions

- `def f(a, b=default, *args, key_only=None, **kwargs)`. Defaults are evaluated once, at definition — never use a mutable default (`[]`, `{}`); use `None` and fill inside. - Return early and flat over nesting deep. Multiple returns are fine; return a tuple for a value-plus-status pair, the shape `llm_chat` itself uses. - Lambdas are for one-expression callbacks (`key=lambda p: p["name"]`), not for named logic
- A function's contract in this codebase is stated in the comment block above it — why it exists, what it refuses, what it returns. Write yours the same way.
## Exceptions

- `try: ... except SomeError as e: ... else: ... finally: ...`. Catch the narrowest exception that names the failure: `json.JSONDecodeError`, `OSError`, `KeyError`, `UnicodeDecodeError`, `subprocess.TimeoutExpired`. - `except Exception` is the codebase's boundary idiom at system edges (a handler must not die on one bad chip) — it belongs at boundaries, not around every call

- Raising: `raise ValueError("plain words naming the problem")`. The bridge's refusals are `ValueError`s whose message is the explanation the operator reads — imitate that: an error message is a sentence a person acts on. - Chain deliberately: a bare `raise` inside `except` re-raises; `raise NewError(...) from e` keeps the cause
- Never swallow silently at a surface the operator sees: catch, name what failed, degrade to the honest fallback (the declared output, the refusal, the empty shelf).
## Context managers

- `with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:` — the file closes on exit, exception or not. Always open text files with an explicit `encoding="utf-8"`. - Modes: `"r"` read, `"w"` write (truncates), `"a"` append, `"x"` exclusive create; add `"b"` for binary (`"rb"`, `"wb"`). PNG work is always binary. - Write your own with `contextlib.contextmanager` when a chip has a setup/teardown pair worth naming.
## Classes, lightly — and dataclasses
- Chips rarely need classes. When state groups naturally, a `@dataclass` is the house-shaped tool:
```python from dataclasses import dataclass, field
@dataclass class Finding: title: str severity: str = "info" tags: list = field(default_factory=list) ```

- Dataclasses give `__init__`, `__repr__` and equality for free; `field(default_factory=...)` is how mutable defaults stay safe. - Plain classes: `class C:` with `__init__(self, ...)` assigning to `self.x`. Methods take `self` first. Keep chip classes shallow — data and one job.
## Typing hints, as the codebase uses them

- Annotate signatures, not every local: `def load(path: str) -> dict:`. Built-in generics are the 3.12 way: `list[str]`, `dict[str, int]`, `tuple[str, int]`, `set[str]`, `str | None` for optionals. - Hints are documentation the interpreter ignores (mostly) — they cost nothing at run time and tell the next reader the shape. `typing.Any` is the honest escape hatch for JSON- shaped data.
## Modules and imports

- `import json`, `from pathlib import Path`. Imports go at the top of the file, stdlib first. A chip's own modules import by their file-set path: `from texttools import count_words` for a sibling, `from. import helpers` only inside package mode (see the runtime document)
- `if __name__ == "__main__":` guards code that should run only when a file is executed directly — inside a chip, `run()` is the entry; module level should declare and define, not act.
# Python reference for chip authors — files, data, and bytes
Written for this pack: a condensed, original reference to the standard-library modules chips reach for when they read, write, hash, pack, and parse. Python 3.12, stdlib only.
## json — reading and writing JSON
How do I read a JSON file in Python? Open it as text with an explicit encoding and hand the file object to `json.load`:
```python import json
with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f: data = json.load(f) ```

- `json.load(f)` parses from a file object; `json.loads(s)` parses from a string. `json.dump(obj, f)` writes to a file; `json.dumps(obj)` returns a string. - `json.dumps(obj, indent=2)` pretty-prints — the shape the bridge writes its own stores in. `ensure_ascii=False` keeps non-ASCII text as-is instead of `\uXXXX` escapes

- JSON parses to plain Python: objects to `dict`, arrays to `list`, strings to `str`, numbers to `int`/`float`, `true` to `True`, `null` to `None`. Trust none of the shapes: check `isinstance(data, dict)` and read with `.get()` — a manifest is outside data until it proves itself. - Bad JSON raises `json.JSONDecodeError` (a `ValueError`). Catch it and name the file in the refusal.
## pathlib and os — paths and files

- `from pathlib import Path`: `p = Path("chips") / name`; `p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")`, `p.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")`, `p.read_bytes()`, `p.write_bytes(b)`; `p.exists()`, `p.is_file()`, `p.suffix`, `p.stem`, `p.parent`; `p.glob("*.png")` lists matches; `p.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` makes directories

- `os.path.join(a, b)`, `os.path.basename(p)`, `os.path.dirname(p)` — the bridge's own idiom; either library is fine, mixing them carelessly is not. - `os.environ` is a dict of the environment: read with `os.environ.get("NAVI_MODEL", "navi")`. A chip receives the operator's whole environment — read what the API promises, leave the rest alone

- `os.listdir(d)` lists a folder (the bridge guards it with try/except and treats failure as an empty folder). - Temp space: `tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="navi-chip-")` makes a private directory; clean it with `shutil.rmtree(tmp, ignore_errors=True)` in a `finally` — the exact discipline `execute_chip` itself uses.
## re — regular expressions

- `re.search(pat, s)` finds anywhere; `re.match` anchors at the start; `re.fullmatch` anchors both ends; `re.findall` returns all matches; `re.sub(pat, repl, s)` rewrites. - Groups: `m.group(1)`, named groups `(?P<name>...)` read as `m.group("name")`. Flags: `re.I` case-insensitive, `re.M` multiline `^`/`$`, `re.S` dot-matches-newline

- Compile once when a pattern runs in a loop: `PAT = re.compile(r"^\s*def\s+run\s*\(")`. Raw strings (`r"..."`) for every pattern — the Studio's own structure checks are four compiled ideas exactly like this. - Escape user text before embedding it in a pattern: `re.escape(text)`.
## datetime — times and stamps

- `datetime.datetime.now()` is naive local time; `datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)` is aware UTC. Never mix naive and aware in a comparison — it raises. - Parse ISO with `datetime.datetime.fromisoformat(s)`; render with `.isoformat()` or `.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M")`; parse a known format with `strptime(s, fmt)`
- `datetime.timedelta(days=1, seconds=30)` does arithmetic; `datetime.date.today()` for dates; `time.time()` is the float epoch when a plain number is what's wanted.
## hashlib — digests
How do I compute a sha256 in Python? Hash the **bytes** with `hashlib.sha256`, read the digest as hex:
```python import hashlib
digest = hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() ```
- `data` must be `bytes` — encode text first: `hashlib.sha256(text.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()`. - Hash a file in chunks so a big file never loads whole:
```python h = hashlib.sha256() with open(path, "rb") as f: for block in iter(lambda: f.read(65536), b""): h.update(block) digest = h.hexdigest() ```

- `hashlib.md5`, `hashlib.sha1`, `hashlib.sha512` share the shape; `h.digest()` returns raw bytes when hex isn't the need. For keyed integrity use `hmac.new(key, msg, hashlib.sha256)` — plain hashes are fingerprints, not signatures.
## zipfile — archives

- Read: `with zipfile.ZipFile(path) as z:` then `z.namelist()`, `z.read("root.py")` (bytes — decode for text), `z.getinfo(name).file_size`. - Write: `zipfile.ZipFile(out, "w", zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED)`, `z.write(file, arcname)` from disk or `z.writestr(arcname, text_or_bytes)` from memory — the bridge's chip export is built on `writestr`
- Treat archive member names as hostile paths: a member with `..` or a leading `/` must never be written to disk as-is.
## struct — binary layouts, and PNG chunks

`struct.pack(fmt, ...)` builds bytes; `struct.unpack(fmt, data)` parses them. Format strings state endianness first: `>` big-endian, `<` little-endian, then codes — `I` unsigned 32-bit, `H` 16-bit, `Q` 64-bit, `B` a byte, `Ns` N raw bytes. `struct.calcsize(fmt)` is the byte count. Network and file formats are big-endian until proven otherwise.

**What Python do I use to write a PNG tEXt chunk?** `struct` for the length, `binascii.crc32` for the checksum — this is exactly how the shipped bridge builds every chunk (`_png_chunk` and `build_cartridge_png` in bridge.py):
```python import binascii, struct
def png_chunk(kind, data): out = struct.pack(">I", len(data)) + kind + data out += struct.pack(">I", binascii.crc32(kind + data) & 0xFFFFFFFF) return out
text_data = b"navi-chip\x00" + json_bytes # keyword, NUL, payload chunk = png_chunk(b"tEXt", text_data) ```

A PNG is the 8-byte signature `b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n"` followed by chunks of *length, type, data, CRC*. The bridge's forge splices its tEXt chunk in right after IHDR (which ends at byte `8 + 12 + 13`). Reading a chunk back is the same walk `parse_cartridge_png` does:

```python pos = 8 while pos + 12 <= len(data): (length,) = struct.unpack(">I", data[pos:pos + 4]) kind = data[pos + 4:pos + 8] chunk_data = data[pos + 8:pos + 8 + length] # ... inspect kind / chunk_data ... pos += 8 + length + 4 ```
Guard every step: a file shorter than its declared chunk is not an error to raise on — it is a `None` to return, the way the shipped parser treats a damaged cartridge.
## sqlite3 — a small real database

- `import sqlite3`; `con = sqlite3.connect(path)`; `cur = con.cursor()`; `cur.execute(sql, params)`; `con.commit()`; close with `with` or `con.close()`. - **Parameters are never string formatting.** Write `cur.execute("SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = ?", (ident,))` — the driver quotes safely; an f-string in SQL is an injection waiting for its input
- `cur.fetchall()` returns tuples; `con.row_factory = sqlite3.Row` makes rows readable by column name. - Create tables defensively: `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ...`

A chip's database lives where the chip says it does — name the path in the chip's description, because the sandbox is wiped after every run: persistent state must live in a real folder (the working directory or a path the operator passes in), never in the sandbox.
# Python reference for chip authors — processes, the network, and house patterns
Written for this pack: a condensed, original reference. Python 3.12, stdlib only. A chip run has a 20-second budget and an operator watching — every pattern here is shaped by that.
## subprocess — running other programs
How do I run a shell command safely from Python? With `subprocess.run` and an argument **list** — never a shell string. The list is the whole safety story, and it is spelled out under the example.
```python import subprocess

proc = subprocess.run( ["nmap", "-sV", target], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=15, ) out = proc.stdout or "" if proc.returncode != 0: # name the failure; proc.stderr holds the tool's own words ... ```

- **The argument list is the safety.** `subprocess.run` with a list passes each element as one argument — no shell ever re-parses it, so an argument containing spaces, quotes, or `;` is data, not syntax. That is how the bridge runs chips themselves. - **Never `shell=True` with text a person or a file supplied.** `shell=True` hands the string to a shell, and every metacharacter in it becomes live

If a command must be displayed, `shlex.join(argv)` renders the list safely; `shlex.split(s)` parses a typed line into a list (the `navi.py` shim's `get_parameters` is built on it). - Always set `timeout=` — an unbounded child inside a 20-second chip run is a timeout that reports nothing. Catch `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` and say what was stopped

- `text=True` decodes output as text; add `errors="replace"` via `encoding=`/`errors=` kwargs when the tool's output encoding is not trustworthy. - `check=True` raises `CalledProcessError` on nonzero exit — prefer reading `returncode` yourself when the output still matters on failure (scan tools report in stderr and exit nonzero for findings, not just failures). - Long-running work does not belong in a chip run
Start nothing you cannot finish and reap inside the budget.
## urllib and http.client — talking HTTP
The standard library's client is `urllib.request`. A JSON POST — the same shape the shipped `navi_internal` stub uses to reach the model server:
```python import json, urllib.request

body = json.dumps({"model": model, "messages": messages}).encode() req = urllib.request.Request( url, data=body, headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"}) with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10) as resp: data = json.loads(resp.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")) ```

- `data=` makes it a POST; no `data` is a GET. Query strings belong in the URL — build them with `urllib.parse.urlencode` and quote path parts with `urllib.parse.quote(part, safe="")`, never by concatenation of raw user text

- **Always pass `timeout=`.** Failures arrive as `urllib.error.HTTPError` (the server answered, with an error status — it carries `.code` and a readable body) and `urllib.error.URLError` (nothing answered). Name which one happened; they have different fixes and the operator deserves to know which

- `http.client` is the lower-level door — reach for it when `urllib` cannot express the request, which for chip work is rare. - A chip's network reach is the operator's machine's reach, under the trust wall: the chip's description must promise every call the code makes
Local-first is the house posture — the model endpoint is local, the Mesh is not a chip surface, and an outside call is a declared behavior, never a surprise.
## threading — usually the wrong tool in a chip

- `threading.Thread(target=fn, args=(...), daemon=True)`, `.start()`, `.join(timeout)`. Shared state needs a `threading.Lock` around it; hand results back through `queue.Queue`, not shared variables. - A chip run is one-shot and budgeted: a thread that outlives `run()` is killed with the subprocess and reports nothing. Prefer doing less, sequentially, inside the budget
When several independent fetches must happen, threads plus a join-with-timeout can fit — but the total still answers to the same 20 seconds, and partial results must be reported as partial.
## House patterns — how Apex's own code writes it
Patterns lifted from the shipped codebase's habits, worth imitating in any chip:
- **Coerce at the border.** `str(x or "")`, `int(x or 0)`, `list(x or [])` — outside data (JSON, payloads, arguments) is normalized the moment it enters, so the body of the code can trust its types

- **Refuse in plain words.** A refusal is a `ValueError` whose message is a complete sentence naming the problem and the fix — "the repo holds several Python files (...) and none is the chip's entry — name the entry file root.py, or add a navi-chip.json manifest naming it." A chip's error output deserves the same craft

- **Degrade to the honest fallback.** When real execution fails, the bridge shows the declared output *with the failure noted* — never a silent substitution, never a swallowed error. Catch at boundaries, keep the tail of the evidence (the bridge keeps the last 1,200 characters), and say what happened. - **Guard the filesystem reads.** `try: ..

except Exception: rows = []` around stores that may not exist yet — absence is a state, not a crash. But a *write* that fails is news: let it raise, or report it by name. - **Comment the why above the function.** The bridge's functions carry a block comment stating what the function is for, what it refuses, and what it returns — the next reader (often Navi herself) navigates by those. Write yours to that standard
- **Print is the interface.** In a chip, output the operator reads is the product: complete sentences, the numbers that matter, nothing that requires the code to interpret.
